Designing an E-Commerce Platform

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Topics: Inventory Consistency, Search, Order Orchestration, Idempotency Asked at: Amazon, Flipkart, Walmart, Meesho Prerequisites:Idempotency and Transactions and Isolation

1. Understanding the Problem

An e-commerce platform lets people find a product among a hundred million of them, put it in a cart, pay, and receive it. The browsing half is a read-scaling problem and it is largely solved by caching. The buying half is where the design earns its difficulty rating, because it has to be correct about two things that cannot be approximated: how many units exist, and how much money changed hands.

The one sentence to say out loud early: you can sell a unit you do not have exactly zero times. Everything structural in this design follows from that. Overselling one PlayStation during a flash sale is not a rounding error you reconcile later, it is a cancelled order, a refund, a support ticket and a customer who buys from someone else next time.

This page is the end-to-end platform. Two neighbouring designs go deeper on their own slice and are not repeated here: Cart Management covers cart persistence, guest-cart merging and cross-device sync, and Payment System covers the payment rails, PSP integration and settlement. Read them alongside this.

Real examples: Amazon, Flipkart, Walmart, Meesho, Shopify, Zalando.

2. Naive First Cut

One application, one database. Products in a table, a stock integer on each row, orders in another table. Search is WHERE title LIKE '%query%'. Checkout reads the stock, checks it in application code, and writes the decremented value.

Why this breaks:

  • The stock check is a race. Two buyers hit checkout at the same moment on a product with one unit left. Both read stock = 1, both decide it is fine, both write stock = 0. Two orders, one unit. This is the lost-update problem and it will happen on your most popular item, under load, in public.💡 Lost update = two requests read the same value, each works out a new value from it, and the second write quietly erases the first. Nothing errors, which is why this bug reaches production. Learn more →
  • LIKE '%query%' is not search. No relevance ranking, no typo tolerance, no faceting by brand or price, and the leading wildcard means no index can be used - it is a sequential scan of 100M rows per query, at 50K queries/sec.
  • One schema cannot hold the catalog. A book has an ISBN and a page count; a t-shirt has a size and a colour; a fridge has a capacity in litres. Modelling that relationally gives you either a table with 400 mostly-null columns or an attribute-value table that every query has to pivot.
  • Checkout has no retry story. The user double-clicks Place Order, or their phone drops the connection and the app retries. Two orders, two charges.
  • Flash sales concentrate everything on one row. Ten thousand concurrent buyers for one SKU (stock keeping unit) all queue on the same row lock.💡 A SKU is one specific purchasable variant - “this shoe, size 9, black” - as opposed to the product, which is “this shoe”. Stock is counted per SKU because that is the thing a warehouse can actually hand over. Throughput collapses to the speed of one lock handoff, and every other order on the site waits behind it.

The rest of this doc evolves that into a platform that cannot oversell, searches properly, and survives a partial failure mid-checkout.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Amazon’s service-oriented split and the Dynamo paper - the 2007 Dynamo paper is the origin of a lot of the industry’s thinking on partitioned, highly available stores, and the broader Amazon lesson is harder-won: separate services by the consistency they require rather than by org chart. Inventory and orders need strong consistency, the catalog does not. (Dynamo: Amazon’s Highly Available Key-value Store, SOSP 2007)
  • Shopify’s flash-sale engineering - published extensively on surviving a single-product traffic spike that is orders of magnitude above baseline, including queueing at the edge and sharding hot inventory counters. Contributes the framing that a flash sale is a load-shedding problem, not just a locking problem. (Shopify Engineering)
  • Temporal and its Cadence lineage from Uber - durable execution for multi-step business processes. Contributes the idea that an order is a long-running workflow with timeouts and compensations, and that the workflow’s state should survive the process that is running it. (Temporal)
  • Debezium - log-based change data capture, which is how the search index and the warehouse learn about catalog changes without the application dual-writing. (Debezium)
  • Elasticsearch - the inverted index, analysis pipeline and relevance scoring that make product search behave the way shoppers expect. (Elasticsearch)

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Browse and search the catalog - find a product among 100M by text query, filter by brand, price and category
  2. Place an order without overselling - a unit is sold at most once, ever, under any amount of concurrency
  3. Track order state - the buyer sees where their order is from placement through to delivery

Below the Line

  • Reviews and ratings
  • Personalised recommendations
  • Seller onboarding and the seller dashboard
  • Returns and refunds workflow
  • Loyalty points and coupons

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

NFR Target
No oversell Hard invariant. Units sold never exceeds units held. Not eventually - never.
Search latency P95 under 200 ms at 50K queries/sec
Order durability A placed order is never lost, even if a downstream service is down
Catalog read scale 1000:1 read-to-write, served mostly from cache and CDN
scroll →

Below the Line

  • Strong consistency on the catalog (eventual is fine; a price change propagating in seconds is acceptable)
  • Real-time stock count on the product page (a stale “In stock” badge is tolerable, a stale reservation is not)
  • Multi-region active-active writes

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Catalog: 100M products, average document ~2 KB → ~200 GB of catalog data, which fits comfortably in a document store with replicas and caches in front.
  • Search: 50K queries/sec. At ~200 ms P95 and a modest fan-out, this is a sharded index problem, not a single-node one.💡 P95 = the time 95% of queries come in under, so it is the experience of the unluckiest 1 in 20 rather than the average. Fan-out means one incoming query becomes several parallel sub-queries - here, one search hitting every index shard and the slowest reply setting the latency.
  • Orders: 5K orders/sec at peak. Each order writes an order row, 2-4 item rows, a reservation row, an idempotency row and an inventory update - about 7 rows, so ~35K row writes/sec. Well within one well-provisioned Postgres primary with partitioning.
  • Flash sale: a single SKU attracting 50K checkout attempts/sec against 1,000 units. Note the ratio: 98% of that traffic is going to fail no matter what you build, so the design goal is to fail it cheaply and fail it fast.
  • Catalog writes: ~1K product updates/sec from sellers (price, stock, description). Every one of those has to reach the search index as well as the catalog store, which turns out to be the hard part.

The shape: an enormous cacheable read path, a modest but strictly correct write path, and one adversarial spike pattern that breaks the modest write path if you do not plan for it.

7. Core Entities

  • Product - the sellable thing: title, description, images, category-specific attributes, seller
  • SKU - a specific purchasable variant of a product (size M, colour blue). Stock is held per SKU, never per product.
  • Inventory - the count of available units for a SKU, plus whatever is currently reserved
  • Reservation - a short-lived, expiring hold on N units of a SKU, created at checkout
  • Cart - the user’s pre-purchase selection, with quantities
  • Order - the immutable record of a purchase, with a state and a captured price
  • Idempotency Key - a client-supplied token that makes a repeated checkout request a no-op

8. API / System Interface

GET /v1/search?q=running+shoes&brand=nike&maxPrice=5000&page=1
  Response: { total, facets: {...}, results: [{ productId, title, price, imageUrl, rating }] }

GET /v1/products/{productId}
  Response: { productId, title, description, attributes, skus: [{ skuId, size, price, inStock }] }

POST /v1/cart/items
  Body: { skuId, quantity }
  Response: { cartId, items: [...], subtotal }

POST /v1/orders
  Headers: Idempotency-Key: <client-generated uuid>
  Body: { cartId, addressId, paymentMethodId }
  Response: { orderId, state: "PAID", total, estimatedDelivery }

GET /v1/orders/{orderId}
  Response: { orderId, state, items: [...], total, timeline: [{ state, at }] }

Security note: The buyer’s identity comes from the session, never from the request body - an endpoint that accepts a userId lets anyone read anyone’s orders. More subtly, price must never be accepted from the client. The server reads the current price at order time and captures it on the order row. A checkout that trusts a client-supplied total is a free-shopping bug, and it is a real one that ships regularly.

9. High-Level Design

Three requirements, three passes. The third one is the whole design.

FR1: Browse the Catalog

100M products with wildly different shapes, read a thousand times for every write.

Why not one relational table. A products table needs columns for every attribute any category might have. Books need isbn and page_count, shoes need size and width, televisions need panel_type and refresh_rate. You end up with either hundreds of nullable columns or an entity-attribute-value side table that turns every product page render into a pivot across dozens of rows. Neither is pleasant, and neither is necessary: a product is naturally a document, and nothing about reading it needs a join.

New components:

  1. Catalog Service - owns product documents. Validates seller writes, serves product reads.
  2. Catalog Store (document DB) - one document per product, with category-specific attributes nested inside it. Read by primary key, which is the only access pattern the product page needs.💡 A document store here is not about “unstructured data” - the data is perfectly structured. It is about the structure differing per category, and about every read being a single-key lookup that a join would only slow down.
  3. CDN plus cache - product pages and images are near-static. At 1000:1 read-to-write, almost every read should be answered before it reaches the Catalog Service.💡 A CDN (content delivery network) keeps copies of pages and images on servers near the shopper, so most product-page views are answered without ever reaching our services. Learn more →

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Shopper opens a product page. The request hits a CDN edge.
  2. On a hit, the page is served in under 30 ms and nothing downstream is touched.
  3. On a miss, the Catalog Service reads the document by primary key and returns it with cache headers.
  4. A seller updating a price writes through the Catalog Service, which invalidates the cached page for that product.

Note what is deliberately not on the product page: a live stock count. Rendering “3 left in stock” requires a read of the inventory tier on every page view, which couples your cheapest path to your most contended one. Show a boolean inStock from a cached value instead and let the truth be established at checkout, where it has to be anyway.

What FR1 leaves broken: it can serve any product whose id you already have, and there is no way in this design to obtain an id. A single-key lookup is the only access pattern the Catalog Store supports, so “running shoes under £80, in stock, 4 stars and up” has no answer here at all. That is FR2. The cached inStock boolean is also, by construction, sometimes a lie – which is a deliberate choice rather than an oversight, and it means FR3 has to treat the badge as advisory and re-establish the truth under a lock.

FR2: Search the Catalog

50K queries/sec with relevance, facets and typo tolerance. The catalog store cannot do this and neither can Postgres.

Why a database cannot serve search. Three separate reasons, and all three are fatal. A leading-wildcard LIKE cannot use a B-tree index, so every query scans. There is no notion of relevance - matching “nike running shoes” should rank a Nike running shoe above a shoe-cleaning kit that happens to mention Nike, and LIKE has no opinion. And a shopper typing “nkie” expects results, which requires fuzzy matching the database has no mechanism for.

New components:

  1. Search Service - translates a shopper’s query and filters into an index query, applies business rules (hide out-of-stock sellers, boost sponsored results).
  2. Search Index (Elasticsearch) - an inverted index over the catalog with an analysis pipeline for tokenising, lowercasing and stemming, plus faceting and relevance scoring. See search indexing for how the inverted index and BM25 ranking actually work.💡 An inverted index flips the data around: instead of “product 42 contains these words”, it stores “the word running appears in these products”, which is what makes a text query fast. Stemming folds “running” and “runs” to one root; faceting is the counts beside each filter; BM25 is the formula that decides which match ranks first. The index now has to be kept current. The straightforward way is for the Catalog Service to write both stores on every product change.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Shopper searches “running shoes” with a brand filter.
  2. Search Service builds an index query with the filter as a facet constraint and returns ranked results plus facet counts.
  3. Separately, a seller updates a product’s price through the Catalog Service, which writes the document to the Catalog Store.
  4. The same request handler then writes the updated document to Elasticsearch.

Search is eventually consistent, and that part is a product decision rather than an accident. Elasticsearch has a refresh interval, so a change is not searchable the instant it is written. A seller who edits a price and immediately searches for their own product may see the old one, and that is fine. What is not fine is the checkout path trusting the index: the price charged and the stock checked must come from the authoritative stores.

What FR2 leaves broken: step 3 and step 4 are two writes to two systems with nothing holding them together, and that is a much worse problem than the refresh interval. The catalog write succeeds and the index write throws, and search serves a stale price indefinitely with nothing anywhere recording that the two have diverged. Worse, two concurrent edits to the same product can reach the two stores in opposite orders, leaving the catalog on version B and the index permanently on version A – no error, no alert, no way to notice except a customer complaint. Retries do not help, because the failure mode that matters is the process dying between the two calls. Deep Dive 4 replaces this with one write.

FR3: Place an Order Without Overselling

This is the design. Everything above was setup.

An order placement has to do several things that span services: confirm the units exist and claim them, charge the buyer, and record an immutable order. Any of those can fail, and the failure cannot leave a unit claimed but unpaid, or a payment taken with no order.

New components:

  1. Inventory Service - the only writer to inventory. Owns the available count per SKU.
  2. Order Service - owns orders and their state machine. Entry point for checkout.
  3. Payment Service - wraps the payment provider.
  4. Inventory Store (Postgres) - strongly consistent and transactional. Holds inventory and orders.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Shopper submits checkout. Order Service captures the current price from the catalog – never from the search index, and never from the client.
  2. Order Service asks Inventory Service whether the units exist. Inventory reads available for the SKU and compares it to the requested quantity.
  3. If there is enough, Inventory writes the decremented value back.
  4. Order Service calls Payment Service and waits for the provider.
  5. On success, it writes the order in state PAID and returns. On failure it calls Inventory to add the units back.

The order state machine. Every state an order can occupy and every legal move between them. Writing it out is what stops an order ending up somewhere nobody designed:

PAID --> REFUNDED is the transition that carries the weight, because PAID is the point at which the buyer’s money has actually moved and every undo after it is a new transaction rather than a rollback.

What FR3 leaves broken: this is the design, and it is wrong in three ways that matter and one that is fatal.

  • It oversells. Steps 2 and 3 are a read, a decision in application code, and a write. Two buyers for the last unit both read available = 1, both decide yes, both write 0. Wrapping it in a transaction does not help – under READ COMMITTED both reads are perfectly legal. This is the fatal one, and Deep Dive 1 is about closing the read-then-write gap and then surviving a flash sale once it is closed.
  • It holds the shopper hostage to the payment provider. Step 3 claims the unit and step 4 then waits seconds on a bank. Anything that goes wrong between them – a process restart, a provider that times out with no callback, a buyer who abandons a 3-D Secure (3DS) redirect – strands the unit with nothing recorded that owes it back.💡 3DS is the step where the bank bounces the shopper to its own page to approve the payment. It is slow and human-paced, which is exactly why holding a database lock across it is untenable. Deep Dive 1 bounds that window; Deep Dive 2 makes the sequence itself survivable.
  • Nothing records where the sequence got to. If Order Service dies after step 4 succeeds and before step 5, the buyer is charged for an order that does not exist. Nobody will refund it, because the only thing that knew a refund was owed was a stack frame. You find these a week later in a finance reconciliation ticket. Deep Dive 2.
  • A double-tap is two orders. The buyer taps Place Order, sees nothing for four seconds, and taps again. Both requests run the whole flow. Two orders, two charges. The Idempotency-Key in the API contract is accepted and ignored. Deep Dive 3.

10. Technology Choices

Tier What it stores Access pattern Primary pick Alternatives
Catalog 100M product documents Single-key read, heavy cache MongoDB DynamoDB, Couchbase, Postgres with JSONB
Search Inverted index over the catalog Fuzzy text, facets, ranking Elasticsearch OpenSearch, Vespa, Solr, Algolia
Inventory and orders Stock counts, reservations, orders, idempotency keys Conditional updates, read-your-writes Postgres MySQL, CockroachDB, Spanner
Cart Per-user cart contents Read-modify-write per user, short-lived Redis with persistence DynamoDB, Memcached
Event bus Order and catalog change events Append-only, replayable, many consumers Kafka Kinesis, Pub-Sub, RabbitMQ
Workflow Order workflow state and timers Durable, resumable, timer-driven Temporal Cadence, Step Functions, Netflix Conductor
scroll →

Why Postgres holds inventory and orders, and not Cassandra or DynamoDB. This is the choice the whole page turns on, and it is the opposite of the reflex answer at this scale.

The oversell invariant needs a conditional update with a reliable affected-row count - “decrement only if the result stays non-negative, and tell me whether you did it.” Postgres gives that in one statement. DynamoDB can do it with a conditional expression on a single item, which works but ties you to one item per SKU and therefore to one partition’s throughput ceiling. Cassandra’s last-write-wins model has no safe read-modify-write at all; lightweight transactions exist but are a Paxos round per operation and explicitly discouraged for hot paths.

The order path also needs read-your-writes, because a buyer who places an order and lands on the confirmation page must see it. And it needs multi-row atomicity: the order row, its item rows and the idempotency key have to commit together or the idempotency guarantee is a lie.

The volume argument that usually pushes people away from relational stores does not apply. 5K orders/sec of small rows is unremarkable for a tuned Postgres primary, and orders partition cleanly by time. Cassandra earns its place on this platform for things like the order event history and per-seller analytics, where volume is high and the access pattern is a partitioned append. It does not belong on the stock count.

Why a workflow engine instead of a chain of queue consumers. You can build an order saga with Kafka and a state column, and plenty of teams do. What you then write by hand is: a timer for every step that might hang, retry with backoff per step, a compensation path per failure mode, and recovery for a process that died between two steps. A workflow engine provides all four as primitives, and the code reads as the business process rather than as a message-handling graph. The cost is another stateful system to operate, which is the honest trade.

11. Data Modeling

Inventory and orders live in Postgres, and the schema is where the correctness guarantees actually live.

-- Stock per SKU. One row per SKU, and the CHECK is the invariant.
CREATE TABLE inventory (
    sku_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    available     INT  NOT NULL,
    reserved      INT  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    version       BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    updated_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    CONSTRAINT available_non_negative CHECK (available >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT reserved_non_negative  CHECK (reserved  >= 0)
);

-- A short-lived claim on units. The sweeper reads expires_at.
CREATE TABLE reservations (
    reservation_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    sku_id         UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES inventory(sku_id),
    order_id       UUID NOT NULL,
    quantity       INT  NOT NULL,
    state          TEXT NOT NULL,   -- HELD, CONFIRMED, RELEASED
    expires_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX reservations_expiry ON reservations (expires_at) WHERE state = 'HELD';

-- Orders. Price is captured here, never read live at fulfilment time.
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    state        TEXT NOT NULL,   -- CREATED, RESERVED, PAID, PACKED, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED, REFUNDED
    total_minor  BIGINT NOT NULL, -- integer minor units, never a float
    currency     CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX orders_by_user ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id        UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    sku_id          UUID NOT NULL,
    quantity        INT  NOT NULL,
    unit_price_minor BIGINT NOT NULL,  -- the price at order time
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku_id)
);

-- Checkout idempotency. The UNIQUE constraint is the whole mechanism.
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
    key          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    order_id     UUID,
    response     JSONB,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
SQL

Three deliberate choices worth defending:

Money is BIGINT in minor units, never a float. A price of 1299.50 is stored as 129950. Floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, and summing a cart in floats produces totals that are off by a paisa in ways customers notice and auditors escalate.

unit_price_minor is on the order item, not read from the catalog at fulfilment. The price the buyer agreed to is a property of the order. A seller changing their price an hour later must not retroactively change what someone was charged.

Orders are indexed by (user_id, created_at DESC) because the dominant query is “my orders, newest first”. Seller-side and ops-side queries have a different shape and are served from a read replica or the warehouse rather than by adding indexes to the write path.

Partitioning. Orders partition by created_at monthly - the table grows forever, queries are overwhelmingly recent, and old partitions can be detached to cold storage. Inventory does not partition by anything useful; it is small (one row per SKU) and the problem is contention on individual rows, not table size. That distinction matters and is covered in Deep Dive 1.

12. Deep Dives

Deep Dive 1: One unit, two buyers, 50K attempts a second. Who gets it?

Problem: A SKU has one unit. Two buyers check out simultaneously. Exactly one must succeed, and this must hold at 50K attempts/sec against the same row.

Bad: steps 2 and 3 of FR3 – read the stock, check it in application code, write the new value.

Buyer A                          Buyer B
-------                          -------
SELECT available  -> 1
                                 SELECT available  -> 1
if (1 >= 1) ok                   if (1 >= 1) ok
UPDATE SET available = 0
                                 UPDATE SET available = 0
COMMIT                           COMMIT

Result: two orders, one unit, available = 0

Both transactions read before either wrote, so neither saw the other. Wrapping this in a transaction does not fix it - under the default READ COMMITTED isolation, both reads are perfectly legal. The bug is the read-then-write gap, not the lack of a transaction.💡 An isolation level is the rule for how much concurrent transactions are allowed to see of each other. READ COMMITTED, the usual default, only promises you never read half-finished writes - it says nothing about a value changing after you read it. Learn more →

steps 2 and 3 of FR3 – read the stock, check it in application code, write the new value.



Both transactions read before either wrote, so neither saw the other. Wrapping this in a transaction does not fix it - under the default isolation, both reads are perfectly legal. The bug is the read-then-write gap, not the lack of a transaction.


 Make the check and the write one atomic statement.




Then inspect the affected row count. One row means you got the unit; zero rows means you did not. The database evaluates and applies the decrement under a row lock it holds for the duration, so there is no window for a second transaction to interleave. , and the constraint is the belt-and-braces guarantee that no code path anywhere can drive it negative.


This is correct. Its limit is throughput: every concurrent buyer for that SKU serialises on one row lock. A lock acquire, update and release is on the order of a millisecond once contention and (WAL) flushes are included, which caps you at roughly a thousand attempts per second for that one SKU. Fine for normal trade. Not fine for a flash sale.


 Reservations, plus shard the hot counter.


Reservations solve the problem, which is the one FR3 walked straight into. Payment takes seconds; holding a row lock for that long is untenable. So the conditional update moves units from to and writes a reservation row with a 15-minute TTL, all in one short transaction. Payment success converts the reservation to a permanent decrement. Payment failure, or TTL expiry caught by a running in the background, returns the units – and that sweeper is the backstop for every case where the thing holding the reservation dies without resolving it.


This adds a state to FR3’s machine: when units are held, on capture, and when the hold expires without payment. That last transition is what returns stock to the market during a live sale, and it is the reason the state machine needs to be a state at all rather than an implementation detail.


Counter sharding solves the problem. Split a stock across N rows:




1,000 units become 20 shards of 50. A buyer picks a shard at random and runs the conditional update against it. Twenty independent row locks means roughly twenty times the throughput, so about 20K attempts/sec. The costs are real and worth stating: the true available count is now a across shards rather than a single read, and a buyer can be told “out of stock” while units remain on a shard they did not try. The standard mitigation is to retry two or three other shards before giving up, and to rebalance shards in the background as they drain unevenly.


Note that 20K/sec is still well short of the 50K attempts/sec in the flash-sale estimate, and that is fine – there were only ever 1,000 units. The point of sharding is not to serve all 50K; it is to resolve the first thousand quickly and reject the rest at a row lock rather than at a queue. Rejecting cheaply is the actual goal.


 Never read the stock and then write it back - ask the database to decrease it only if there is enough, in one instruction, and check whether it actually did. For checkout, don’t take the unit away permanently until payment clears; put a 15-minute hold on it instead. And if one product is so popular that everyone is fighting over the same database row, split its stock into twenty rows so twenty people can be served at once.


 a payment can hang indefinitely - a bank redirect the user abandons, a payment service provider (PSP) timing out with no callback. Without a TTL those units are stranded until a human notices. Fifteen minutes is long enough for any legitimate payment flow and short enough that abandoned carts return stock to the market while the sale is still live.




Deep Dive 2: The process dies after the charge and before the order. Who refunds the buyer?


Problem: Placing an order touches inventory, payment and fulfilment. Each is a separate service with its own database. Any step can fail, time out, or succeed-but-not-reply, and the result must never be a unit claimed with no payment, or money taken with no order.


Bad: FR3’s bare sequence of calls, where the only record of progress is the stack frame of the request handler.
Claim the units, charge the buyer, write the order. At 5K orders/sec, a deploy that rolls pods mid-afternoon kills some number of in-flight checkouts at step 4, and every one of those is a charge with no order and no refund owed to anyone in writing. There is no retry, no compensation, and no way to even enumerate the damage afterwards – the orders table has no row for an order that never got written.
The intuitive fix is a distributed transaction across all three with two-phase commit, and it is worth being clear about why that is not on the table.💡 Two-phase commit (2PC) is the classic “all or nothing across several databases” protocol: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare and hold its locks, then tells them all to commit. The holding-locks part is what makes it unusable here. 2PC requires every participant to hold locks through the prepare phase until the coordinator decides, so an inventory row stays locked while a payment provider thinks about it – exactly the multi-second lock Deep Dive 1 just worked to eliminate. A coordinator crash after prepare leaves participants blocked, holding locks, unable to decide alone. And the payment provider is a third party over HTTP; it will not enlist in your transaction at all. 2PC is not an option here regardless of whether it is a good idea. 2PC requires every participant to hold locks through the prepare phase until the coordinator decides - so an inventory row stays locked while a payment provider thinks about it, which is exactly the multi-second lock you were trying to avoid. A coordinator crash after prepare leaves participants blocked, holding locks, unable to decide alone. And the payment provider is a third party over HTTP; it will not enlist in your transaction at all. 2PC is not an option here regardless of whether it is a good idea.
 FR3’s bare sequence of calls, where the only record of progress is the stack frame of the request handler.


Claim the units, charge the buyer, write the order. At 5K orders/sec, a deploy that rolls pods mid-afternoon kills some number of in-flight checkouts at step 4, and every one of those is a charge with no order and no refund owed to anyone in writing. There is no retry, no compensation, and no way to even enumerate the damage afterwards – the orders table has no row for an order that never got written.


The intuitive fix is a distributed transaction across all three with two-phase commit, and it is worth being clear about why that is not on the table. 2PC requires every participant to hold locks through the prepare phase until the coordinator decides, so an inventory row stays locked while a payment provider thinks about it – exactly the multi-second lock Deep Dive 1 just worked to eliminate. A coordinator crash after prepare leaves participants blocked, holding locks, unable to decide alone. And the payment provider is a third party over HTTP; it will not enlist in your transaction at all. 2PC is not an option here regardless of whether it is a good idea. 2PC requires every participant to hold locks through the prepare phase until the coordinator decides - so an inventory row stays locked while a payment provider thinks about it, which is exactly the multi-second lock you were trying to avoid. A coordinator crash after prepare leaves participants blocked, holding locks, unable to decide alone. And the payment provider is a third party over HTTP; it will not enlist in your transaction at all. 2PC is not an option here regardless of whether it is a good idea.


 A saga - a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action for the earlier steps.




Each step commits locally, so no lock is held across a service boundary. The catch is that compensation is not a rollback. A refund is a new transaction that happens the charge was real, so there is a window where the buyer’s statement shows a charge for an order that no longer exists. That window has to be short and the messaging has to be honest. See for the orchestration-versus-choreography trade.


 An orchestrated saga on a durable workflow engine.


Hand-rolled sagas fail in a specific, predictable way: the process running the saga dies between step two and step three. The charge happened, nothing recorded that it happened, and no compensation will ever run because the thing that knew to run it is gone. You discover these as a finance reconciliation ticket a week later.


A persists the workflow’s state and its position after every step. If the worker dies mid-saga, another worker resumes from the last completed step. Timers, retries with backoff, and compensation handlers are declared rather than coded, and they survive deploys and crashes.


The workflow drives the order state machine from FR3, now with the state Deep Dive 1 added. Two transitions carry the weight: on hold expiry, which the sweeper owns, and , which is the compensation path that has to exist because is the point of no return for the buyer’s money. Every transition is explicit, so an order can never be in a state nobody designed.


 You cannot wrap “take the stock, take the money, create the order” in one database transaction, because the payment company is not part of your database. So do each step separately, record where you are after each one, and if a later step fails, run the undo for the earlier ones. Keep that progress record in something that survives a server crash, otherwise a crash halfway through leaves a charge nobody will ever refund.




Deep Dive 3: The buyer taps Place Order twice. How many charges?


Problem: The buyer taps Place Order, nothing visibly happens for four seconds, and they tap again. Or the response is lost to a dropped connection and the app retries automatically. The server receives two identical checkout requests and must create one order and one charge.


Bad: what FR3 does, which is read the Idempotency-Key header and throw it away. Each request is treated as new.
Two orders, two reservations, two charges, from a buyer who did nothing wrong. This is one of the most common real-world e-commerce bugs because it is invisible in testing - you do not double-tap your own checkout button on a fast local network, and the four-second pause that provokes the second tap only exists once a real payment provider is in the path.
 what FR3 does, which is read the header and throw it away. Each request is treated as new.


Two orders, two reservations, two charges, from a buyer who did nothing wrong. This is one of the most common real-world e-commerce bugs because it is invisible in testing - you do not double-tap your own checkout button on a fast local network, and the four-second pause that provokes the second tap only exists once a real payment provider is in the path.


 A client-supplied idempotency key with a uniqueness constraint.


The client generates a UUID per checkout (not per request - a retry reuses it) and sends it as a header. The server inserts it into , whose primary key is the key itself. The second insert violates the constraint, the server catches that, and rejects the duplicate.


This stops double orders. Its weakness is what the duplicate request receives: a constraint-violation error is not the right answer. The buyer’s retry gets a failure for an order that actually succeeded, so they try again, and now they are genuinely confused about whether they bought anything.


 Write the key inside the same transaction as the order, store the response, and replay it.




The key and the order commit together, so there is no state where the key exists but the order does not. On a duplicate, the server reads the stored and returns it with the original status code. The retry is indistinguishable from the first call, which is what idempotency actually means - not “rejects duplicates” but “the second call has the same effect and the same answer as the first”.


Two operational details that matter. , or one customer’s key collides with another’s and leaks an order. And - 24 hours is typical - because keeping them forever grows a table that is only useful for minutes. State the window in your API docs so clients know when a retry stops being safe.


 Have the app make up a unique code for each checkout attempt and send it with every retry. Save that code in the database in the same transaction as the order. If the same code shows up again, don’t make a second order - look up what you answered the first time and say exactly that again. The customer’s retry then just works instead of erroring.


See for the general pattern and its variations.




Deep Dive 4: A seller edits a price. How does the search index find out?


Problem: Product data lives in the catalog store and must also be in Elasticsearch. These are two separate systems, and a write has to reach both.


Bad: the dual-write FR2 built - the Catalog Service writes to the catalog store, then writes to Elasticsearch.
At ~1K product updates/sec, you do not need an unusual failure rate for this to matter: a 0.1% index-write failure is one silently stale product per second, accumulating, with no mechanism anywhere that would ever notice. Every partial failure leaves the two divergent. The catalog write succeeds and the index write fails, so search shows a stale price indefinitely with nothing to detect it. Or the index write succeeds and the catalog write rolls back, so search advertises a product that does not exist. Retrying the index write helps with transient failures and does nothing for the case where the process dies between the two calls. Worse, two concurrent updates to the same product can reach the two systems in opposite orders, so the catalog ends up with version B while the index has version A, permanently, with no error anywhere.
 the dual-write FR2 built - the Catalog Service writes to the catalog store, then writes to Elasticsearch.


At ~1K product updates/sec, you do not need an unusual failure rate for this to matter: a 0.1% index-write failure is one silently stale product per second, accumulating, with no mechanism anywhere that would ever notice. Every partial failure leaves the two divergent. The catalog write succeeds and the index write fails, so search shows a stale price indefinitely with nothing to detect it. Or the index write succeeds and the catalog write rolls back, so search advertises a product that does not exist. Retrying the index write helps with transient failures and does nothing for the case where the process dies between the two calls. Worse, two concurrent updates to the same product can reach the two systems in opposite orders, so the catalog ends up with version B while the index has version A, permanently, with no error anywhere.


 The outbox pattern. The application writes the product change and an event row to the catalog store in one transaction; a relay reads the outbox and publishes to the index.


Now there is exactly one atomic write, so the event cannot be lost and cannot exist without the data. The costs are application code in every write path and an outbox table you have to drain and prune. See .


 Log-based change data capture.


Instead of the application announcing its own changes, read the database’s own replication log. Debezium acts as a replication client, converts each committed change into an event with before and after images, and publishes to Kafka. An indexer consumes the topic and writes to Elasticsearch.


What this buys over the outbox: no application change at all, every change captured including ones made by a migration script or a DBA, and strict per-row ordering straight from the log. It also gives you a clean reindex path - rewind the Kafka consumer offset and replay, or run Debezium’s initial snapshot to rebuild the index from scratch without touching the application.


The consumer must be idempotent, because CDC delivers . Indexing is naturally idempotent if you use the product id as the document id and include a version so an out-of-order replay cannot overwrite newer data with older. See for the snapshot-then-stream handover and the schema-evolution hazard.


 Don’t have your code write to the database and then to the search index - sooner or later one of those two writes fails and the two disagree forever with nobody noticing. Instead, let a tool watch the database’s own change log and copy every change into the search index. Your code only ever writes to one place, and the copying is somebody else’s reliable job.




13. Design Self-Audit



 
 

 Question
 Answer
 

 
 
 

 Payment succeeds but the order write fails?
 The workflow owns this. Payment capture and order commit are separate steps with the order write retried on resume; if it cannot be completed, the compensation refunds. The charge is never left without either an order or a refund.
 

 

 Can a buyer see their own order immediately?
 Yes. Orders are written to the Postgres primary and the confirmation read goes to the primary, not a replica. This is why the order store is not eventually consistent.
 

 

 Flash sale on one SKU?
 Shard that SKU’s stock across N rows (Deep Dive 1), queue or rate-limit checkout at the edge, and fail the 98% of attempts that cannot succeed early and cheaply rather than letting them reach Postgres.
 

 

 Price changes between add-to-cart and checkout?
 The order captures unit_price_minor at order time. The cart shows an indicative price and the checkout page re-reads the authoritative one, so the buyer is shown any change before they confirm.
 

 

 What is strongly consistent, what is eventual?
 Strong: inventory, reservations, orders, idempotency keys - all in one Postgres boundary. Eventual: the search index, the product page cache, analytics, and recommendations.
 

 

 Reservation sweeper fails?
 Units stay held until it recovers, which costs sales but never correctness. The sweeper is idempotent and stateless, so it is safe to run several and to re-run after a gap.
 

 

 Single points of failure?
 Postgres primary is the real one. Mitigate with synchronous replication to a standby and automated failover; accept that a failover window blocks order placement while browsing continues to serve from cache.

14. Core Flows


Flow: Checkout End to End




Walkthrough:


    
 
  1. Checkout arrives with an idempotency key. A repeat of a key already seen returns the stored response immediately and none of the following happens.
    2. 
 
  2. Order Service reads the authoritative price, writes the order as CREATED, and starts the workflow. Order and key commit together.
    3. 
 
  3. The workflow reserves units. Inventory runs the conditional update and writes a reservation with a TTL.
    4. 
 
  4. On success the workflow charges the buyer, then confirms the reservation into a permanent decrement and moves the order to PAID.
    5. 
 
  5. On payment failure the workflow releases the reservation and cancels the order, and the units are immediately back on sale.
    6. 
 
  6. Out of stock short-circuits before any payment attempt.
    7. 



Non-obvious failure: the workflow charges the buyer successfully and then the worker dies before confirming the reservation. The charge is real, the order is still RESERVED, and the reservation TTL is ticking. If nothing intervenes, the sweeper releases the units for an order that has been paid for - selling the same unit twice, which is the exact thing this design exists to prevent. Two defences, and you want both: the workflow engine resumes the workflow on another worker and completes the confirmation, and the sweeper refuses to release a reservation whose order is in state PAID, escalating it for manual resolution instead. The sweeper checking order state before releasing is the one that saves you when the workflow engine itself is the thing that failed.


Flow: Search Query




Walkthrough:


    
 
  1. The query and filters go to Search Service, which builds an index query.
    2. 
 
  2. Elasticsearch returns ranked product ids and facet counts, not full documents.
    3. 
 
  3. Search Service hydrates only the page being shown - twenty documents - from the Catalog Service, which answers from cache.
    4. 
 
  4. An empty result set triggers a fuzzy retry so a typo returns suggestions instead of a blank page.
    5. 



Non-obvious failure: the index returns a product id that the catalog no longer has, because a deletion propagated to the catalog but not yet to the index. Hydration returns nothing for that id. Dropping it silently from the page is the right behaviour - it gives nineteen results instead of twenty rather than a broken tile or an error - and the mismatch should increment a metric, because a rising rate of it means CDC is lagging or broken.




15. Final Architecture




How it works end-to-end (browse and search path):


    
 
  1. Shopper opens a product — the CDN serves the page and images, and the Catalog Service is only touched on a miss
    2. 
 
  2. Shopper searches — Search Service queries the inverted index for ranked ids and facets, then hydrates only the visible page from the cached catalog
    3. 
 
  3. Seller updates a product — the write lands in the Catalog Store, and CDC streams the change into the search index within seconds
    4. 



How it works end-to-end (buy path):


    
 
  1. Cart edits — held in Redis, cheap to write and tolerable to lose
    2. 
 
  2. Checkout — Order Service dedupes on the idempotency key, captures the price, writes the order, and starts a durable workflow
    3. 
 
  3. Units reserved — Inventory Service runs a conditional update against Postgres and holds the units with a TTL
    4. 
 
  4. Payment — on capture, the reservation converts to a permanent decrement and the order becomes PAID; on failure the workflow releases the hold and cancels
    5. 
 
  5. Expired holds — the sweeper returns units from abandoned checkouts, refusing to touch anything whose order is already paid
    6. 





Key Technologies



 
 

 Term
 What it is
 

 
 
 

 Conditional update
 A single UPDATE ... WHERE available >= n whose affected-row count tells you whether it applied. The primitive that prevents oversell.
 

 

 Reservation
 A short-lived, expiring claim on stock, created at checkout and resolved by payment or by TTL.
 

 

 Saga
 A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, used instead of a distributed transaction across services.
 

 

 Durable workflow
 A long-running process whose state and position persist, so a crash resumes rather than stranding the work. Temporal, Cadence, Step Functions.
 

 

 Idempotency key
 A client-supplied token stored with the order, making a retried checkout return the original response rather than creating a second order.
 

 

 CDC
 Change data capture. Reading the database’s own replication log to publish every committed change downstream.
 

 

 Inverted index
 The term-to-document mapping that makes ranked, faceted, typo-tolerant text search possible.

What’s Expected at Each Level


Mid-level


Split the platform into services and justify the split. Identify that stock is held per SKU, not per product. Spot the read-then-write race on inventory and fix it with a single conditional update, checking the affected row count. Propose a search index separate from the catalog store and explain why LIKE cannot do the job. Recognise that checkout needs an idempotency key.


Senior


Explain why reservations exist - that payment takes seconds and you cannot hold a row lock across it - and design the TTL plus sweeper. Choose a saga over two-phase commit and name the compensating actions. Draw the order state machine and defend every transition. Explain why inventory and orders belong in a strongly consistent store while the catalog and search can be eventual, and why dual-writing to the index is wrong - reaching for outbox or CDC. Store money as integer minor units and capture price at order time.


Staff+


Address the flash sale directly: shard the hot SKU counter, accept the false-negative rate it introduces, and shed load at the edge rather than at the database.💡 Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests early, at the cheapest layer, so the expensive layer stays healthy. In a flash sale 98% of attempts cannot succeed anyway, so turning them away at the edge is kinder than letting them queue on a database row. Learn more → Explain what happens when a saga crashes between charging and confirming, and why the sweeper must check order state before releasing - the two independent defences for the one failure that causes a genuine double-sell. Discuss CDC operationally: snapshot-then-stream handover, idempotent consumers, replay for reindexing, and schema evolution breaking downstream consumers. Be explicit about the Postgres primary as the remaining single point of failure and what a failover costs.




🎯 Key Takeaways


    
 
  • One atomic conditional update is what prevents oversell - not a transaction wrapper, and never a read followed by a write
    • 
 
  • Reservations with a TTL convert the multi-second payment window into a short, bounded claim on stock
    • 
 
  • A saga on a durable workflow engine survives the crash that strands a hand-rolled saga mid-charge
    • 
 
  • Idempotency means replaying the original response, not rejecting the duplicate with an error
    • 
 
  • CDC beats dual-writing for keeping search in sync, because the application then has exactly one place to write
    • 
 
  • Money is an integer in minor units, and price is captured at order time - two small schema decisions that prevent a whole class of incident
    •
